1052:
Step 1: Configure NAT on R2 (Task 1)

Create the standard named ACL matching traffic sourced from R3's link to R2, then configure PAT (NAT overload) translating that traffic to R2's Ethernet0/0 address, and mark the inside/outside interfaces.

```
R2(config)#ip access-list standard PUBNET
R2(config-std-nacl)#permit host 10.2.3.3
R2(config-std-nacl)#exit
R2(config)#ip nat inside source list PUBNET interface Ethernet0/0 overload
R2(config)#interface Ethernet0/1
R2(config-if)#ip nat inside
R2(config-if)#exit
R2(config)#interface Ethernet0/0
R2(config-if)#ip nat outside
R2(config-if)#exit
```

Step 2: Configure NTP (Task 2)

Make R1 the NTP time source and point R2 at it as a client only (no peer relationship), using R1's Ethernet0/2 address, then set the clock on R1, the NTP server.

```
R1(config)#ntp master 1
R2(config)#ntp server 10.1.3.1
R1(config)#end
R1#clock set 00:00:00 1 may 2018
```

Step 3: Configure DHCP (Task 3)

On R1, exclude the first ten addresses of the pool with a single command, then create the DHCP pool. On R3, obtain the Ethernet0/2 address from that pool via DHCP.

```
R1(config)#ip dhcp excluded-address 10.1.3.1 10.1.3.10
R1(config)#ip dhcp pool NETPOOL
R1(dhcp-config)#network 10.1.3.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)#exit
```

```
R3(config)#interface Ethernet0/2
R3(config-if)#ip address dhcp
R3(config-if)#no shutdown
R3(config-if)#exit
```

Step 4: Configure SSH from R1 to R3 (Task 4)

On R3, set a domain name (required before RSA keys can be generated), create the local account, generate a 1024-bit RSA key pair, and restrict the vty lines to SSH only so telnet and other remote protocols are excluded.

```
R3(config)#ip domain-name ccna-lab.local
R3(config)#username netadmin secret N3t4ccess
R3(config)#crypto key generate rsa modulus 1024
R3(config)#ip ssh version 2
R3(config)#line vty 0 4
R3(config-line)#transport input ssh
R3(config-line)#login local
R3(config-line)#exit
```

Verify from R1:

```
R1#ssh -l netadmin 10.1.3.11
```

Step 1: Configure the local account on Gw1 (Task 1)

Restrict the vty lines to telnet only, and create a local Scrypt-hashed account at privilege level 1 (user EXEC), matching the task's 'Privilege level: Exec mode' requirement.

```
GW1(config)#username wheel privilege 1 algorithm-type scrypt secret lock3path
GW1(config)#line vty 0 4
GW1(config-line)#transport input telnet
GW1(config-line)#login local
GW1(config-line)#exit
```

Step 2: Configure and apply the extended named ACL on Gw1 (Task 2)

Re-enter the existing named ACL to append entries without disturbing what's already there, permit BOOTP/DHCP and HTTPS, log everything else with full detail, and apply the ACL inbound on the VLAN 10 subinterface.

```
GW1(config)#ip access-list extended CORP_ACL
GW1(config-ext-nacl)#permit udp any any eq 67
GW1(config-ext-nacl)#permit udp any any eq 68
GW1(config-ext-nacl)#permit tcp any any eq 443
GW1(config-ext-nacl)#deny ip any any log-input
GW1(config-ext-nacl)#exit
GW1(config)#interface Ethernet0/0.10
GW1(config-subif)#encapsulation dot1Q 10

GW1(config-subif)#exit
```

Step 3: Configure DHCP Snooping on Sw1 (Task 3)

Enable snooping globally and for VLAN 10, disable option-82 insertion, keep MAC-address verification on, and trust the two inter-switch uplinks (the HostA access port stays untrusted).

```
SW1(config)#ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)#ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
SW1(config)#no ip dhcp snooping information option
SW1(config)#ip dhcp snooping verify mac-address
SW1(config)#interface range Ethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)#ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if-range)#exit
```

Step 1: Configure reachability to the SW1 LAN subnet in router R2 (Task 1)

```
R2(config)#ip route 192.168.0.0 255.255.255.0 Ethernet0/0 10.10.31.1
```

Step 2: Configure default reachability to the Internet subnet in router R1 (Task 2)

```
R1(config)#ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 Ethernet0/0 10.10.13.3
```

Step 3: Configure a single, redundant static route to the Internet subnet in router R2 (Task 3)

A default route is not allowed on R2, so point a specific static route at R1's loopback instead of an exit interface. Since R1's loopback is reachable over OSPF via both R1-R2 links, this gives redundancy across both links without pinning the route to a single interface.

```
R2(config)#ip route 172.20.20.128 255.255.255.128 10.10.1.1
```

(R1's loopback 10.10.1.1/32 is assumed to be advertised into OSPF, giving R2 two equal/available paths to it.)

Step 4: Configure the primary/floating-backup route to the SW1 LAN in router R1 (Task 4)

The primary route exits Ethernet0/1 with the default static administrative distance (1); the backup route exits Ethernet0/2 with a floating AD of 2, so it is only used if the primary route fails.

```
R1(config)#ip route 192.168.0.0 255.255.255.0 Ethernet0/1 10.10.12.2
R1(config)#ip route 192.168.0.0 255.255.255.0 Ethernet0/2 10.10.12.130 2
```
1134:
Step 1: Configure R1

Enter configuration mode, create the loopback interfaces, and bring up the two point-to-point links to R2 and R3. R1's own IP on the link it shares with R2 (10.0.12.0 /24 in this exercise, using the topology's 10.10.12.0/24 segment) is used as its OSPF router ID, per Task 1.

```
conf terminal
interface Loopback0
ip address 10.10.1.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Ethernet0/0
no shut
ip address 10.10.12.1 255.255.255.0
ip ospf 1 area 0
duplex auto
!
interface Ethernet0/1
no shut
ip address 10.10.13.1 255.255.255.0
ip ospf 1 area 0
duplex auto
```

Under the OSPF process, set the router ID and advertise Loopback0 (already a /32, so a host wildcard is its natural match) and Loopback1. Task 3 requires Loopback1 to be advertised using a host wildcard mask (0.0.0.0), not the /24 wildcard that matches its configured subnet mask.

```
router ospf 1
router-id 10.10.12.1
network 10.10.1.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
network 192.168.1.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
!
copy run start
```

Step 2: Configure R2

R2's own IP on the link it shares with R1 becomes its router ID (Task 1). Both of R2's links toward R1 and R3 get the maximum OSPF priority (255) so R2 wins DR election on each segment, per Task 2. Loopback1 again uses a host wildcard mask.

```
conf terminal
interface Loopback0
ip address 10.10.2.2 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
ip address 192.168.2.2 255.255.255.0
!
interface Ethernet0/0
no shut
ip address 10.10.12.2 255.255.255.0
ip ospf priority 255
ip ospf 1 area 0
duplex auto
!
interface Ethernet0/2
no shut
ip address 10.10.23.2 255.255.255.0
ip ospf priority 255
ip ospf 1 area 0
duplex auto
!
router ospf 1
router-id 10.10.12.2
network 10.10.2.2 0.0.0.0 area 0
network 192.168.2.2 0.0.0.0 area 0
!
copy run start
```

Step 3: Configure R3

R3's links facing R2 keep the default priority (no priority command), so R1 and R3 remain eligible only as DROTHER on that segment, satisfying Task 2's requirement that they stay at default. Loopback1 again uses a host wildcard mask for Task 3.

```
conf t
interface Loopback0
ip address 10.10.3.3 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
ip address 192.168.3.3 255.255.255.0
!
interface Ethernet0/1
no shut
ip address 10.10.13.3 255.255.255.0
ip ospf 1 area 0
duplex auto
!
interface Ethernet0/2
no shut
ip address 10.10.23.3 255.255.255.0
ip ospf 1 area 0
duplex auto
!
router ospf 1
network 10.10.3.3 0.0.0.0 area 0
network 192.168.3.3 0.0.0.0 area 0
!
copy run start
```

Step 4: Disable the R1-R3 link's ability to accept additional OSPF neighbors

Task 4 asks to lock the R1-R3 link so no other OSPF routers can join it. Setting the OSPF network type to point-to-point on both ends removes the broadcast-network DR/BDR behaviour, which is what allows arbitrary extra routers to attach and form adjacencies on that segment.

On R1:
```
conf t
interface Ethernet0/1
ip ospf network point-to-point
end
copy run start
```

On R3:
```
conf t
interface Ethernet0/1
ip ospf network point-to-point
end
copy run start
```

Step 5: Clear the OSPF process and verify

Because the router ID and priority changes were applied to an OSPF process that may already have formed adjacencies, the process must be cleared for the changes (new router IDs, new DR election) to take effect, as Task 2 explicitly calls out.

```
clear ip ospf process
show ip ospf neighbor
```

Confirm the reset when prompted. R2 should appear as DR in the neighbor table on both the R1 and R3 sides.

1182:
Step 1: Subnet 172.16.0.0/16 for 16 sites and configure Sw101 and Sw102

16 sites requires exactly 16 subnets. Since 16 = 2^4, only 4 bits need to be borrowed from the host portion, which keeps as many host bits as possible (maximizing hosts per subnet) while still meeting the requirement. The new prefix is /16 + 4 = /20 (mask 255.255.240.0), giving a block size of 16 in the third octet: 172.16.0.0/20, 172.16.16.0/20, 172.16.32.0/20, and so on.

The second subnet is 172.16.16.0/20, covering 172.16.16.0-172.16.31.255. Its first usable address is 172.16.16.1 and its last usable address is 172.16.31.254.

On Sw101 (first usable address):
```
enable
configure terminal
interface e0/0
ip address 172.16.16.1 255.255.240.0
no shutdown
end
```

On Sw102 (last usable address):
```
enable
configure terminal
interface e0/0
ip address 172.16.31.254 255.255.240.0
no shutdown
end
```

Step 2: Subnet 2001:DB8::/50 for 16 sites and configure IPv6 addressing

The same 16-subnet requirement applies: borrowing 4 bits (2^4 = 16) from the 14 bits available between /50 and the standard /64 boundary keeps the interface-ID space as large as possible, giving a new prefix of /50 + 4 = /54. The borrowed 4 bits sit in the fourth hextet; each subnet increases that hextet by 0x0400. The first subnet is 2001:db8:0:0::/54, and the second subnet is 2001:db8:0:400::/54 (covering 2001:db8:0:400:: through 2001:db8:0:7ff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff).

Any address in that block with a unique 64-bit interface identifier satisfies the task; ::1 and ::2 are used here.

On Sw101:
```
enable
configure terminal
interface e0/0
ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:400::1/54
end
```

On Sw102:
```
enable
configure terminal
interface e0/0
ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:400::2/54
end
```

1295:
Step 1: Subnet 10.20.0.0/16 for 16 sites and assign the second subnet's endpoints

16 required subnets need 4 extra bits (2^4 = 16), so /16 becomes /20 -- the minimum subnetting needed, which maximizes the host bits per subnet (4094 usable hosts each). The /20 subnets step by 16 in the third octet: 10.20.0.0/20, 10.20.16.0/20, 10.20.32.0/20, and so on. The second subnet is 10.20.16.0/20, usable range 10.20.16.1 - 10.20.31.254.

On Sw101:
```
interface e0/0
no switchport
ip address 10.20.16.1 255.255.240.0
no shutdown
```

On Sw102:
```
interface e0/0
no switchport
ip address 10.20.31.254 255.255.240.0
no shutdown
```

Step 2: Subnet 2001:db8::/52 for 16 sites and assign GUAs on the second subnet using EUI-64

16 required subnets again need 4 extra bits, so /52 becomes /56 -- the minimum subnetting needed, maximizing the remaining bits for host addressing. The /56 subnets step through the high nibble of the 4th hextet: 2001:db8:0:0::/56, 2001:db8:0:100::/56, 2001:db8:0:200::/56, and so on. The second subnet is 2001:db8:0:100::/56; since EUI-64 always derives a 64-bit interface identifier, the address is applied on the interface with a /64 mask.

Step 1: Configure dynamic one-to-one NAT on R2 for R3-to-R1 traffic

Standard ACL XLATE matches all of R3's own addresses (its interface facing R2, its loopback, and its interface facing R1) so any traffic sourced from R3 gets translated.  permit 10.1.3.11
 exit
interface Ethernet0/1
 ip nat inside
 exit
interface Ethernet0/0
 ip nat outside
 exit

Step 1: Local telnet-only account on Sw101 (Task 1)

"Privilege level: Exec mode" is user EXEC = privilege 1 (the `username` command's default level, stated explicitly here for clarity), and vty access is restricted to telnet only.
```
Sw101(config)#username support privilege 1 password max2learn
Sw101(config)#line vty 0 4
Sw101(config-line)#transport input telnet
Sw101(config-line)#login local
Sw101(config-line)#exit
```

Step 2: Named extended ACL ENT_ACL on Sw101 (Task 2)

The rule order matters - each host-specific exception has to come before the broader rule it's carving an exception out of, and the ACL needs an explicit trailing permit since the implicit deny-all at the end of every ACL would otherwise break "allow all other traffic from VLAN 200":
```
Sw101(config)#ip access-list extended ENT_ACL
Sw101(config-ext-nacl)#deny icmp host 192.168.200.10 host 192.168.100.10
Sw101(config-ext-nacl)#permit tcp host 192.168.200.10 any eq 23
Sw101(config-ext-nacl)#deny tcp any any eq 23
Sw101(config-ext-nacl)#permit ip any any
Sw101(config-ext-nacl)#exit
```
Applied inbound on the VLAN 200 SVI, so it filters traffic as it arrives from VLAN 200 (this assumes Sw101 is doing inter-VLAN routing between VLAN 100/200 with SVIs already preconfigured, per the lab's "preconfigurations applied" note, since that's the only way PC1<->PC2 traffic would reach Sw101 to be filtered at all):
```
Sw101(config)#interface Vlan200
Sw101(config-if)#ip access-group ENT_ACL in
Sw101(config-if)#exit
```

Step 3: Port security on Ethernet0/0 of Sw102 (Task 3)

"No notification action" (drop silently, no syslog/SNMP trap, no counter) is exactly what violation mode `protect` does - `restrict` would still send a notification, so it's the wrong mode here. Dynamic learning is the default behavior once port security is enabled, so no `sticky` keyword is needed since the task doesn't ask addresses to persist in the config.
```
Sw102(config)#interface Ethernet0/0
Sw102(config-if)#switchport mode access
Sw102(config-if)#switchport port-security
Sw102(config-if)#switchport port-security maximum 4
Sw102(config-if)#switchport port-security violation protect
Sw102(config-if)#exit
```
1337:
Step 1: IPv4 - subnet 10.30.64.0/19 for 64 sites, maximize hosts (Task 1)

64 sites need exactly 64 subnets. 64 = 2^6, so borrow 6 bits: new prefix /19 + 6 = /25 (255.255.255.128) - that divides the /19 into exactly 64 subnets of 128 addresses (126 usable hosts) each, using the fewest possible borrowed bits for the required count, which is what "maximize hosts" means here. The subnets run 10.30.64.0/25, 10.30.64.128/25, 10.30.65.0/25, ... The second subnet is 10.30.64.128/25 (range .128-.255), first usable .129, last usable .254.
```
Sw101#configure terminal
Sw101(config)#interface e0/0
Sw101(config-if)#ip address 10.30.64.129 255.255.255.128
Sw101(config-if)#no shutdown
Sw101(config-if)#end
```
```
Sw102#configure terminal
Sw102(config)#interface e0/0
Sw102(config-if)#ip address 10.30.64.254 255.255.255.128
Sw102(config-if)#no shutdown
Sw102(config-if)#end
```

Step 2: IPv6 - subnet 2001:db8::/56 for 64 sites, maximize hosts (Task 2)

Same 64-subnet requirement: borrow 6 bits from /56, new prefix /62. Those 6 bits land in the low byte of the 4th hextet, so each subnet increments that hextet by 4 (2001:db8:0:0::/62, then 2001:db8:0:4::/62, ...). The second subnet is 2001:db8:0:4::/62. The task's "64-bit interface identifier" refers to the last 64 bits of the address (hextets 5-8) - use any value that's unique between the two switches within that subnet.
```
Sw101#configure terminal
Sw101(config)#interface e0/0
Sw101(config-if)#ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:4::1/62
Sw101(config-if)#no shutdown
Sw101(config-if)#end
```
```
Sw102#configure terminal
Sw102(config)#interface e0/0
Sw102(config-if)#ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:4::2/62
Sw102(config-if)#no shutdown
Sw102(config-if)#end
```

Step 2: OSPF process 33, router-id = E0/1's address (Task 1)

R1(config-router)#router-id <the address you read off Ethernet0/1 in Step 1>
R1(config-router)#exit

Step 3: Bring up OSPF toward R2 and R3 without network statements, and force R1 to always win the DR election (Task 2)

Each interface joins Area 0 with the interface-level `ip ospf` command instead of a `network` statement under the process (as required), and priority 255 - the maximum - guarantees R1 outranks R2/R3 as long as they're left at the default priority of 1:
```
R1(config)#interface <the interface facing R2, from Step 1>
R1(config-if)#ip ospf 33 area 0
R1(config-if)#ip ospf priority 255
R1(config-if)#exit
R1(config)#interface <the interface facing R3, from Step 1>
R1(config-if)#ip ospf 33 area 0
R1(config-if)#ip ospf priority 255
R1(config-if)#exit
```

```
R1#show ip ospf neighbor
R1#show ip ospf interface brief
```
